title: When the Adult Kids Go “No Contact”
author: Juliana Chan Erikson
summary: Juliana Chan Erikson's WORLD feature, linked in Trevin Wax's 'Trevin's Seven' roundup, examines family estrangement from the perspective of parents whose adult children have cut off contact. Anchored by the stories of MeDenne Jones, Aimee Palmer, Amy McCullough, and Deborah Satonick, the piece cites Karl Pillemer's estimate that about 27 percent of American adults are estranged from a family member and traces how Murray Bowen's 1975 concept of 'emotional cutoff' has shifted into a culturally endorsed solution promoted by YouTube coaches. It sets parents' tendency to blame third parties such as boyfriends, spouses, or therapists against a Together Estranged survey in which most estranged adult children cite emotional abuse or narcissism. The analytical core comes from two therapists: Paul Hokemeyer says there is no definitive evidence estrangement is rising, only more language and social permission, while Julie Hamilton reports clients told to 'put up boundaries' in ways that turn boundaries into barriers. Both agree abuse warrants protection but that good clinicians treat estrangement as a last resort, and the piece ends with grief likened to a death and a small story of reconciliation.
points: Pillemer's research puts family estrangement at about 27 percent of American adults, and the cultural framing has moved from Bowen's 'coping mechanism' to going no contact as a solution.

Parents in support groups most often blame a third-party relationship for the break, while a Together Estranged survey found 81 percent of estranged adult children cited psychological or emotional abuse.
Therapist Paul Hokemeyer argues there is no definitive evidence of higher estrangement rates, only greater visibility and social permission to talk about it.
Therapist Julie Hamilton warns that 'boundaries' is often misapplied to justify cutting off relationships entirely, when protection from harm does not always require exclusion.
Parents describe estrangement as grieving a death, and the reconciliations reported began with shared vulnerability, reflection, and small concrete openings such as exchanging a phone number.
quotes: Family estrangement—cutting off all contact with parents or a family of origin—is not new. Psychiatrist Murray Bowen first coined the term “emotional cutoff” in 1975 to describe a coping mechanism for someone struggling with unresolved emotional issues.

Most members blame a relationship with a third party—a boyfriend, a spouse, in-laws, sometimes even a therapist—as the catalyst for the estrangement. Occasionally parents and children will split over political or religious differences, or after one comes out as gay or transgender.
Not surprisingly, estranged children see the situation differently, and they are more likely to blame family strife for their departure.

No definitive evidence shows that adult children are going no contact with parents at dramatically higher rates than in previous generations,” said Paul Hokemeyer, a licensed marriage and family therapist in New York. “What has changed is the language, visibility, and social permission to discuss it openly.

It’s one thing to walk out of the room when your family talks politics, or not to call your alcoholic father on the nights he goes out for drinks. It’s another when boundaries become barriers, Hamilton said.
Therapy at its best should neither reflexively prescribe estrangement nor pressure a vulnerable person back into a relationship that remains harmful,” added Hokemeyer.
Some children do reconnect. Parents said sharing problems with a trusted person helps, as does reflecting on the relationship and working on communication skills.
